claims.text: The heterostructure contains scale-spanning phase distributions.
The heterostructure contains distinct interfacial regions.
A surrogate model will integrate imaging-derived microstructural descriptors with mechanical-testing data.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs local stress distributions.
The hierarchical heterostructure governs interphase load transfer.
The morphology and spatial distribution of phases mediate local deformation.
The morphology and spatial distribution of phases mediate crack propagation.
Encoding hierarchical microstructural features in a reduced-order model can predict macroscopic mechanical behavior more rapidly than computationally intensive multiscale simulations.
The surrogate model will predict Young's modulus under the prescribed tensile-test conditions.
The surrogate model will predict yield strength under the prescribed tensile-test conditions.
The surrogate model will predict fracture-related responses under the prescribed fracture-test conditions.
The surrogate model may provide approximately a tenfold prediction-speed increase over established simulations.
The surrogate model may reduce prediction-error margins by approximately 10–15% relative to conventional approaches.

Very high strain rates, extreme temperatures, or processing-induced deviations from the characteristic hierarchy may weaken the relevant microstructure–property correlations and cause the model to fail.
Model success depends on the accuracy and resolution of the microstructural descriptors.
